analysis.one_liner: Raises bankruptcy protections for workers' wages, pensions, and union contracts and limits executive pay in corporate bankruptcies.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House Judiciary subcommittee by an 8-4 vote in September 2010 but never received a full committee vote or a vote by the full House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company goes bankrupt, workers and retirees often stand in line behind banks and executives. This bill would raise the amount of unpaid wages and benefits that get first claim on a bankrupt company's assets, make severance pay a priority, let workers and unions recover lost pension and 401(k) value in fraud cases, and make it much harder for a company to use bankruptcy to dump union contracts and retiree health benefits. It would also bar big exit bonuses and allow courts to claw back executive pay when companies cut worker benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees of companies that file for bankruptcy. They would recover up to $20,000 in unpaid wages and benefits as a top-priority claim, keep severance and layoff pay, and gain new ways to recover pension and retirement-plan losses. Union members would gain stronger protections against having their contracts torn up in bankruptcy, and courts would have to weigh job and benefit preservation when approving asset sales.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles to $20,000 the priority claim for unpaid wages, salaries, and benefit-plan contributions, and removes the 180-day limit on the look-back period [S2][S3].
Makes severance pay owed under a company policy or union contract an administrative expense, meaning it is treated as earned in full and paid near the front of the line [S2][S3].
Allows workers and unions to claim pension shortfalls when a defined-benefit plan is terminated, and 401(k) stock losses when the employer committed fraud or breached a duty to participants [S2][S3].

Rewrites the rules for rejecting collective bargaining agreements, requiring good-faith negotiation, limiting concessions to the minimum essential to exit bankruptcy, and requiring clear and convincing evidence before a court can approve rejecting a union contract [S3].

Bars approval of payments, exit bonuses, and incentive compensation to insiders and top executives unless they are part of a program generally applicable to all employees and are not excessive compared to what nonmanagement workers received, and lets courts recover a matching percentage of executive pay when workers' contracts or retiree benefits are cut [S2][S3].

Requires bankruptcy courts, when approving a sale of company assets, to consider whether a bidder offered to keep jobs, preserve employment terms, and assume pension and retiree health obligations [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Executives of failing companies, who would lose exit bonuses and incentive pay and face clawbacks; secured lenders and investors, who would see worker claims take a larger share of recoveries and could no longer waive certain wage-payment obligations by agreement; and distressed companies, which would face higher costs and stricter limits on cutting union contracts and retiree benefits during reorganization.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate executives, secured lenders, distressed companies

drawbacks.text: Higher priority claims for wages, severance, and layoff damages, plus new surcharges against secured lenders, could make lending to or investing in distressed companies riskier and more expensive, potentially pushing marginal firms toward liquidation rather than reorganization [S2][S3].

The rewritten rules for modifying union contracts and retiree benefits add negotiation steps, presumptions against the company, and a higher evidentiary bar, which employers and creditors argued could make reorganizations slower and harder, reducing the value of companies and the recoveries available to all creditors [S3].
Executive pay restrictions and clawbacks could make it harder for troubled companies to retain the managers needed to run a reorganization, a standard objection to such limits [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully shift money and bargaining power in bankruptcies from executives and lenders toward workers and retirees, which is its purpose. The costs are real: more expensive and slower reorganizations, greater risk for lenders to distressed firms, and some chance that stricter rules lead to liquidations rather than restructurings that save jobs. How large those costs would be is contested; the bill's design tries to limit concessions to the 'minimum essential' to keep a company alive, but courts would bear a heavy burden applying the new standards.

outcome.mechanism: It got a subcommittee hearing and the subcommittee voted 8-4 to send it to the full House Judiciary Committee, but the committee never acted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on February 24, 2010, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, which held a hearing on May 25, 2010 [S5].
On September 15, 2010, the subcommittee forwarded an amended version to the full committee by a vote of 8-4 [S5].
The full Judiciary Committee never voted on the bill, and it never received a House floor vote before the 111th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and secured lenders at distressed companies, and firms that use bankruptcy to shed union contracts and retiree benefits, kept the existing bankruptcy rules that the bill would have tightened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Executives and lenders kept the old rules

for.name: John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-MI), sponsor and Chairman of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up 17 original cosponsors.

for.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on May 25, 2010 and voted 8-4 on September 15, 2010 to forward an amended version to the full committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill after the subcommittee forwarded it, leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

against.name: 4 members of the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law
against.what_they_did: Voted against forwarding the bill to the full committee on September 15, 2010.

sides.party_line_note: All 58 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsors appear in the record; the subcommittee's 8-4 vote to advance the bill, with 4 noes, is consistent with a partisan split, though the record does not list the noes by party.

industries.industry: Executives and senior managers of bankrupt companies
industries.note: The bill would bar exit bonuses and incentive pay for insiders and top executives unless shared generally with workers, and would let courts recover a matching percentage of executive pay when union contracts or retiree benefits are cut. Its interest ran against workers' recovery in bankruptcy.

Unpaid post-filing wages and benefits would become a charge against secured lenders' collateral that they could no longer waive by agreement, and higher worker priority claims would reduce their recoveries.

Stricter limits on rejecting union contracts and cutting retiree benefits would raise reorganization costs, though some firms that reorganize rather than liquidate might benefit from the bill's job-preservation emphasis.
